newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan cuts soybean crushing, eyes soyoil imports.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan cuts soybean crushing, eyes soyoil imports.

text.p: Taiwan's hog crisis has begun hitting the island's edible oil producers, who said on Wednesday a fall in demand for soy-based feed was forcing them to cut production and turn to oil imports.
Soybean crushing yields two main products, oil and soymeal. Crushing to produce oil would result in a fast-growing surplus of meal for which there is no demand, crushers explained.
"The massive pig slaughter has significantly reduced feed demand for soymeal, forcing processors to cut volume," Hui Shung Agriculture and Food Co buyer Jack Lee told Reuters.
Lee said soy crushing yields about 80 percent soymeal and 17 percent soyoil, so soymeal accumulates at a much faster rate than soyoil -- an economically untenable situation.
Traders said excess soymeal inventories already had slowed overall soyoil and soymeal production by 10 percent.
"Taiwan's soybean crushing volume already dropped by about 10 percent," spokesman Liu Chin-jen of Taiwan's largest soybean crusher, Ttet Union Corp, told Reuters.
Liu said Ttet was preparing to halt its soybean crushing line for up to a week, but said the shutdown was for regular maintenance.
Liu declined to give details of Ttet's production volumes and inventories, but traders estimated it could crush 3,000 tonnes of soy daily and store about 15,000 tonnes of soymeal.
Traders said most soybean processors already had reduced or temporary halted their crushing operations.
An executive at Taiwan Chia Hsin Flour Feed and Vegetable Oil Corp said his firm had temporarily halted its soybean process line due to excess soymeal inventories.
In 1996, Taiwan imported about 2.4 million tonnes of soybeans, which could produce 1.9 million tonnes of soymeal and 400,000 tonnes of soyoil after crushing, traders said.
Taiwan also imported about 30,000 tonnes soyoil and some soymeal in 1996, they added.

The independent newsletter Oil World said on Tuesday that Taiwan was producing less soyoil and lard between October 1996 and September 1997, which should bring higher imports of palm oil, soyoil, sun oil and tallow.
Total vegetable oil and animal fats import demand was forecast at 287,000 tonnes in the October to September period, up 40,000 tonnes from the year-earlier period.
Taiwan on March 20 ordered a pork export ban and mass slaughter of all pigs at affected farms after confirming an oubreak of foot and mouth disease.

As of late on Tuesday, the deadly contagion had been detected on 1,465 of the island's 25,000 farms with officials projecting that 1.22 million pigs would have to be destroyed. Only 340,808 had been slaughtered and 60,299 died to date.
Taiwan's pork export ban could lead to a 10 percent fall in soybean imports, due to declining demand for feed.
Taiwan soybean crushers have said they were considering exporting soymeal to China but prices made this unattractive.
Taiwan soymeal would cost about US$360 a tonne for delivery at China's coastal areas, higher than U.S. soymeal at US$350 levels, traders said.
Taiwan's soymeal protein level is between 43 to 44 percent.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has projected China's 1996/97 soymeal imports at 1.3 million tonnes, up from 1.1 million in 1995/96 and near zero prior to that.
China, once a significant exporter, now imports soymeal to cover soaring consumption for animal feed.
-- Taipei Newsroom (2-508-0815)
